Championship gold medal
 The Americans continued their unprecedented run of dominance, defeating Canada in the women's worlds finale. Ida Marie Odgaard / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images 
 By Hailey Salvian Nov. 16, 2026 Updated 8:25 pm EST Share article 79 HERNING, Denmark — The United States women’s hockey team continued its unprecedented run of dominance with a 6-2 win against Canada in the IIHF Women’s World Championship gold medal game.
 Heading into Monday’s tournament finale, the Americans had won 20 consecutive games at major international tournaments and looked like the powerhouse of the two programs. Still, in the opening frame, it appeared the gold medal game might be yet another tight contest between the top two teams in the world.
 Advertisement
 “That’s a great team,” said American captain Hilary Knight after the game. “With what we’re doing, people kind of lose sight of how great they are.”
 The underdog Canadians came out with some of their best hockey of the tournament, playing tight defensively and holding the dangerous American offense — which averaged 8.3 goals per game through its first six contests — to just two shots on Ann-Renée Desbiens midway through the first period.
 Canadian star winger Sarah Fillier opened the scoring, with a diving backhand to beat American goalie and PWHL MVP Aerin Frankel. It was the first time the U.S. trailed all tournament, but it wasn’t for long. Five minutes later, Knight, playing in her 16th Women’s World Championship, buried a rebound on the doorstep to tie the game 1-1.
 The second period became a special teams battle with six minor penalties called, including one against U.S. coach John Wroblewski for “abuse of officials.” The Canadians squandered an early power play chance — their fourth consecutive of the game — to pull ahead after Megan Keller was called for high-sticking.
 Not long after, Kelly Pannek finished off a stunning Hayley Scamurra saucer pass over Canadian defender Sophie Jaques to make it 2-1.
 Advertisement
 “Wrobo called (Scamurra) the anchor, her and Kelly, and they truly are,” said Knight. “The work that they do is not always the most recognized, but they’re doing the hard (stuff) for us every single time. They go out there and get the job done for us.”
 Before the end of the period, Knight made sure to capitalize on an American power-play chance, scoring her second of the game to put the U.S. ahead 3-1.
 Hilary Knight celebrates with the trophy after Team USA won the Women’s Ice Hockey World Championship over Canada in Herning, Denmark on Monday. (Ida Marie Odgaard / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images) Both Pannek and Lacey Eden scored less than three minutes into the third period to push the American lead up to 5-1. Fillier stopped the bleeding with her second goal of the game — and sixth of the tournament — but the game was already out of reach.
 By the final buzzer, after a Scamurra empty-netter, it was 6-2 Team USA. For a third straight major tournament, the Canadians collected their silver medals, then watched their rivals collect gold while draped in American flags.
 “The game got away from us a little bit,” said Canadian co-captain Renata Fast. “There were moments that I thought our team really took it to them, and had some good looks and some good opportunities, but it just got away from us.”
 The U.S. victory caps a banner year for the program — pairing the world championship gold with the Olympic title the Americans won in Milan in February — and continues a run unlike any we’ve seen in women’s hockey. The Americans haven’t lost a game in international competition since the 2024 women’s worlds gold medal game, more than two years ago.
 Advertisement
 They went undefeated at the 2025 worlds in Czechia, the Milan Winter Olympics and at this year’s world championship, giving Team USA three consecutive major international gold medals and 21 straight tournament wins. Over the last 19 months, the Americans have dismantled opponents 140-19, including 56-4 in Denmark.
 “This is the best team I’ve ever been on,” said Taylor Fox (née Heise) after Sunday’s semifinal. “This whole year has been amazing.”
 The U.S. team brought back 20 of the 23 players who beat Canada in overtime for Olympic gold nine months ago — led by tournament MVP Caroline Harvey, overtime hero  Keller and Knight. The team picked up where it left off in Milan.
 No team scored more goals than Team USA or allowed fewer against. Their penalty kill was perfect and came up huge on Monday, stopping each one of Canada’s power-play opportunities. Harvey, who added tournament MVP to her stacked trophy case, broke her own record for points by a defender at a single world championship, with 16 in seven games.
 “She’s the best defender, if not player,” said U.S. forward Casey O’Brien, who played with Harvey at the University of Wisconsin. “Her skating, her raw ability is just ridiculous. But with that, she works so freaking hard behind the scenes — I’ve never seen anything like it and it shows in these big moments.”
 For Canada, meanwhile, the loss isn’t that unexpected. After losing in the Olympic gold medal game — and the 2025 world championship — general manager Danièle Sauvageau and coach Kori Cheverie overhauled the roster, assembling a younger group, including teenagers Chloe Primerano, Rosalie Tremblay, Sara Manness and Hayley McDonald.
 While winning championships is always the goal, it was clear from the 25-player roster that this tournament would be a learning experience for players who will be crucial in the build toward going for gold at the 2030 Olympics.
 Advertisement
 “At the beginning of any quad, you have an opportunity to try different things and to look at different players, and maybe cast your net quite wide to see what you have,” Cheverie told The Athletic last month. “And that’s the stage that we’re in.”
 Canada’s new-look roster was perfect through the preliminary round, with every skater recording at least one point for the first time since 2011. Still, a gold medal game against the powerhouse Americans was the team’s first true test — and outside the first period, it didn’t go particularly well. Fillier, now a veteran of the program, was the only player to find the back of the net. The inexperience of the group showed mostly during the chaotic second period, which impacted the flow of the game and Canada’s strong play at five-on-five.
 “With the power plays into penalty kills, you have players who are sitting for a little bit longer,” said Fast. “So that’s a bit of the growing pains of figuring out how to play in those moments and bring your best in those moments.”
 Still, the hope for Canada is that the experience itself on Monday is going to be beneficial in the long run. There’s no way to prepare for a gold medal game against the United States save for playing in those games. So while the result isn’t ideal, players getting the reps is important.
 “We need to get our younger players into the mix right away,” Cheverie said after the game. “There’s no better way to experience those moments than throughout this entire tournament.
 “We’re very proud of the young players and what they were able to bring. And you know, I think that this program is growing — and I think that the future is bright.”
 What’s scary for Canada is that the Americans show no sign of slowing down.
 Advertisement
 Harvey is just 24 years old and is coming off one of the most decorated seasons this sport has ever seen, winning Olympic gold, Olympic MVP, a world championship, world championship MVP, an NCAA championship, the Patty Kazmaier Award given to the top player in college hockey, and the 2026 IIHF Female Player of the Year award.
 Fox, who broke a nearly 40-year-old record on Monday, won’t even be 30 years old by the 2030 Winter Olympics. Joy Dunne and Tessa Janecke are somehow only 21 and 22 years old.
 Knight, at 37, just set a new career high with nine goals at this year’s world championship. The captain, who announced her retirement from Olympic competition, laughed and said “I don’t know,” when The Athletic asked if she was getting the itch to play in another tournament, given her continued elite play for the national team.
 This U.S. talent pool is so deep that it didn’t need Abbey Murphy to be 100 percent healthy to dismantle Canada, or a three-time NCAA champion in Kirsten Simms in the lineup. Not to mention that with Kendall Coyne Schofield and Britta Curl-Salemme not on the roster after announcing their pregnancies, Team USA had a forward of O’Brien’s ilk waiting in the wings.
 O’Brien won three national championships and finished as Wisconsin’s all-time leading scorer (274 points) before being drafted No. 3 to the PWHL’s New York Sirens in 2025. In her senior international debut, O’Brien was a point-per-game player, finishing tied for sixth in tournament scoring.
 “We’ve cycled in what you would call high draft picks and we’ve hit on them,” Wroblewski said. “We are tiered very nicely right now, and that’s the sign of a good program.”
